lesson.intro: Some interviews ask you to design the classes for a parking lot, a library or an elevator instead of solving an algorithm problem. This lesson shows how those rounds run, how to turn a vague prompt into requirements and use cases, how to find classes and relationships and sketch them as a text diagram, how SOLID guides the design, and four worked designs: a parking lot, a library, an elevator at a high level and an LRU cache API.
objectives: Run an object-oriented design round: clarify requirements, write use cases and manage the time
Turn use cases into classes, responsibilities and relationships, and sketch them as a text class diagram
Apply SOLID so the parts most likely to change are easy to extend
Design and code a parking lot, a library system and an O(1) LRU cache, and outline an elevator
Recognize and avoid the most common object-oriented design interview mistakes

sections.title: How an object-oriented design round runs
sections.body:
"Design a parking lot." "Design a library system." "Design the classes for an elevator." Prompts like these open an **object-oriented design** round, also called low-level design. Not every internship process includes one (coding problems are far more common for interns), but some companies use it, and the same skills come up whenever an interviewer asks "how would you structure this?" after a coding problem, and in your first weeks on a real codebase.

OOD is not system design. System design asks how services, databases, caches and queues fit together to serve many users. OOD stays inside one program: which classes exist, what each one is responsible for, how they relate, and what their methods look like. Nobody expects load balancers in a parking lot answer.

A typical round lasts 45 to 60 minutes and runs roughly like this:

- **Requirements, about 5 to 10 minutes.** Ask questions, agree on scope, list the main use cases.
- **Core objects, about 10 minutes.** Name the classes, their key fields and how they relate, and sketch a class diagram in the editor.
- **Code the core, about 15 to 20 minutes.** Write the important classes and the methods behind the main use cases. Skip trivial getters; write the interesting logic.
- **Extend and discuss, the rest.** The interviewer changes something ("now add electric vehicle charging", "two members want the same book") to see whether your design bends or breaks.

What interviewers look for:

- **Clarifying before designing.** The prompt is vague on purpose.
- **Sensible abstractions.** Classes that match real concepts, each with one clear job.
- **Clean relationships.** Composition for has-a, inheritance only for a genuine is-a.
- **Extensibility.** A new vehicle type or pricing rule should mean adding code, not rewriting it.
- **Working code and communication,** with the same think-out-loud habits as any coding round.

There is no single right answer. Two strong candidates can produce different class lists; what matters is that every choice has a reason you can say out loud.
sections.code:
A 45-minute OOD round

 0-8   Requirements: questions, scope, use cases
 8-18  Core classes, fields, relationships, diagram
18-38  Code the core classes and main methods
38-45  Changes, edge cases, trade-offs, testing
sections.tip: Say the plan at the start: "I'll ask a few questions, list the use cases, sketch the classes, then code the core." Interviewers relax when they can see where you are going.
sections.pitfall: Treating OOD like system design and drawing servers, databases and load balancers. Stay inside one program unless the interviewer asks you to zoom out.

check.question: Which question belongs in an object-oriented design round rather than a system design round?
choices: How many database replicas do we need for 10 million users?
Should ParkingLot or Spot decide whether a vehicle fits?
Which load balancer algorithm spreads the traffic best?
How do we shard the users table across regions?
check.explanation: OOD is about classes, responsibilities and methods inside one program, such as which class owns the fit rule. Replicas, load balancing and sharding are system design questions about services and infrastructure.

sections.title: Gathering requirements and use cases
sections.body:
A vague prompt is a test. "Design a parking lot" could mean a three-spot driveway or an airport garage with ten levels, valet parking and monthly passes. Candidates who start drawing classes immediately usually design the wrong thing, then spend the round patching it.

Spend the first several minutes turning the prompt into a short list of requirements. Useful questions fall into a few groups:

- **Actors:** who uses the system? Drivers, attendants, administrators, a payment terminal?
- **Core use cases:** what must they be able to do? Park, leave and pay, see free spots, add a level.
- **Variations:** what kinds of things exist? Vehicle sizes, spot types, membership levels, book formats.
- **Rules:** what constraints apply? Can a motorcycle use a car spot? Is there a loan limit? How is the fee calculated?
- **Scope:** one lot or many? Is payment processing part of this, or someone else's service?

Write the answers down as **use cases**, short sentences in the form "actor does action", and read them back to the interviewer. They become your checklist for the rest of the round, and the verbs in them become methods.

Separate **functional requirements** (what the system does: issue a ticket, compute a fee) from **non-functional** ones (how well: fast lookups, safe when two cars arrive at once). Functional requirements drive the classes. Non-functional ones show up as choices, such as a dictionary for O(1) lookups or a lock around spot assignment.

When something is out of scope, say so and leave a seam: "I'll treat payment as an interface with a `charge(amount)` method, so a real processor can plug in later." That shows judgment without spending ten minutes on credit cards. And when the interviewer says "your call", make the assumption explicit: "I'll assume one entrance, three spot sizes and hourly pricing rounded up." A stated assumption is a decision; an unstated one is a surprise later.
sections.code:
Prompt: "Design a parking lot."

Q  Several levels?             A  Yes.
Q  Which vehicles?             A  Motorcycle, car, van.
Q  Can a car use a big spot?   A  Yes, if no car spot is free.
Q  How is the fee computed?    A  Per started hour; may change.
Q  Is card payment in scope?   A  No, treat it as external.

Use cases
- Driver parks: the lot assigns the smallest free spot
  that fits and issues a ticket
- Driver leaves: the lot frees the spot, returns the fee
- Attendant sees how many spots of each size are free
- Admin adds a level of spots
sections.tip: Ask which change is most likely ("pricing may change" above). It tells you exactly where an abstraction will pay off.
sections.pitfall: Asking twenty questions and never converging. Five or six questions, a short use-case list read back to the interviewer, then move on.

check.question: The interviewer says payment processing is out of scope. What is the best way to handle payment in your design?
choices: Ignore payment completely, with no mention of it
Design a full credit card processing module anyway
Define a small Payment interface such as charge(amount) and treat the real processor as external
Ask the interviewer to design the payment part
check.explanation: A thin interface leaves a seam where a real processor plugs in, and it costs one line. Ignoring payment leaves the leave-and-pay use case incomplete, and building it all wastes the time you agreed to spend elsewhere.

sections.title: Classes, responsibilities and relationships
sections.body:
With use cases written down, find the objects. A quick, reliable method is **noun and verb analysis**: underline the nouns in your use cases as candidate classes and the verbs as candidate methods, as in the code block for a library.

Not every noun deserves a class. Ask whether it has its own data and behavior. "Due date" is just a field of Loan. "Librarian" may be only a role with permissions unless librarians behave differently in your use cases. Watch for the classic split between a **Book** (title, author and ISBN, one per title) and a **BookCopy** (one physical item on a shelf that can be lent). Merging them makes "how many copies are free?" awkward and loans ambiguous.

Give each class **one clear responsibility**, and put behavior next to the data it needs. "Is this loan overdue?" belongs on Loan, which holds the due date, not on Library. When a method mostly reads another object's fields, it probably lives in the wrong class.

Then name the relationships:

- **Inheritance (is-a):** a subclass that can stand in anywhere its parent is used. ElectricSpot is a Spot.
- **Composition (has-a, owns):** the part lives and dies with the whole. A ParkingLot owns its Levels; remove the lot and its levels go with it.
- **Aggregation (has-a, shares):** the parts exist on their own. A Team has Members who can leave and join other teams.
- **Association (uses or knows):** one object refers to another. A Loan knows its Member and its BookCopy.
- **Multiplicity:** how many of each. One Book has many BookCopies; each BookCopy has at most one active Loan.

Fixed sets of values, such as vehicle sizes or elevator states, should be **enums**, not strings: `Size.LARGE` cannot be misspelled, and anyone reading the code can see every option. Small values compared by content, such as Money or a Location, make good immutable dataclasses.

Prefer a few well-named classes over many. Every class you add is one more thing to explain in the time you have.
sections.code:
Use case: "A member borrows a copy of a book;
each loan has a due date."

Noun        Decision
member      class Member
book        class Book: title, author, ISBN
copy        class BookCopy: one physical item
loan        class Loan: copy, member, due date
due date    a field of Loan, not a class
library     class Library: copies, checkout

Verb        Method
borrows     Library.checkout(isbn, member)
returns     Library.return_copy(loan)
is overdue  Loan.is_overdue(today)
sections.tip: For every method, ask "which object has the data this needs?" and put the method there. It settles most "where does this go?" debates.
sections.pitfall: Using inheritance for has-a. A ParkingLot is not a kind of Level, and a Car is not a kind of Engine; inheriting gives one class another's whole interface and couples them tightly. Hold the part as a field instead.

check.question: In a library design, why model Book and BookCopy as separate classes?
choices: Python does not allow one class to have both a title and an ID
A title (one per ISBN) and a physical copy that can be lent are different things; one Book has many copies, and loans attach to copies
It doubles the number of classes, which interviewers reward
BookCopy must inherit from Book to share the title
check.explanation: Loans, availability and condition belong to individual copies, while title and author belong to the book. Keeping them apart makes "how many copies are free?" and "who has copy c2?" simple. A copy has a book (association); it is not a kind of book.

sections.title: Class diagrams in text
sections.body:
Interviews rarely give you a diagram tool, and you do not need one. A plain-text class diagram in the shared editor is quick, readable and easy to change while you talk.

Two parts are enough:

- **Class boxes:** the class name, then its key fields with a leading `-` (internal) and its public methods with a leading `+`, with simple types. List what matters for the use cases, not every getter.
- **Relationship lines:** one line per relationship, using UML-style arrows. `A <|-- B` means B inherits from A. `A *-- B` means A owns B (composition). `A o-- B` means A has B but does not own it (aggregation). `A --> B` means A uses or refers to B (association). Put multiplicities in quotes next to a side: `"1"`, `"0..1"`, or `"*"` for many.

The code block shows the parking lot from the next sections. Read top to bottom, it tells the story of the design in seconds: the lot owns its spots and tracks tickets, pricing is a pluggable interface with two implementations, and each spot holds at most one vehicle.

Habits that help:

- **Draw before you code,** but only the main classes. Five boxes and seven lines are plenty; the diagram is a map, not the territory.
- **Point at it while you talk:** "A Ticket links a vehicle to a spot and a start time, so `leave` can find the spot from the plate."
- **Update it when the design changes.** If the interviewer adds electric charging, add ElectricSpot and its line, then talk about what changes in the code.
- **Walk each use case across it.** Which object receives the call, and which objects does it talk to? A use case with no clear home means a missing method or class.

The notation in the code block follows Mermaid's class diagram syntax closely, so if you want a rendered picture for a README later, these lines need little editing.
sections.code:
classDiagram
class ParkingLot {
  -spots: list[Spot]
  -pricing: Pricing
  -active: dict[str, Ticket]
  +park(vehicle, now) Ticket
  +leave(plate, now) int
}
class Spot {
  -id: int
  -size: Size
  -vehicle: Vehicle
  +fits(vehicle) bool
}
class Pricing {
  +fee(hours) int
}
ParkingLot "1" *-- "*" Spot
ParkingLot o-- Pricing
ParkingLot --> Ticket
Ticket --> Spot
Spot --> "0..1" Vehicle
Pricing <|-- Hourly
Pricing <|-- MemberFree
sections.tip: Keep the diagram at the top of the editor and the code below it. When the interviewer asks a question, you can point at both.
sections.pitfall: Drawing every class you can imagine before writing any code. A diagram with fifteen boxes and no methods behind them reads as avoiding the hard part.

check.question: In the text diagram, what does `Pricing <|-- Hourly` mean?
choices: Pricing inherits from Hourly
Hourly owns a Pricing object
Hourly inherits from Pricing (Hourly is a kind of Pricing)
Pricing calls Hourly once an hour
check.explanation: The hollow triangle points at the parent, so Hourly is the subclass. Ownership is drawn with *-- (composition) and plain use with -->.

sections.title: SOLID applied to a design
sections.body:
SOLID is easiest to use in an OOD round as a set of questions you ask about your own design. Here is how each principle shows up in the parking lot.

- **Single responsibility:** does each class have one reason to change? If ParkingLot also computes fees, a pricing change and a layout change both edit the same class. Move pricing into its own object.
- **Open/closed:** can you add a variation without editing working code? An if-chain on vehicle type inside a fee function grows with every new rule. A Pricing interface with one class per rule means a new rule is a new class.
- **Liskov substitution:** can every subclass stand in for its parent? If ElectricSpot's `fits()` raised an exception for gas cars instead of returning False, any loop over spots would crash. Subclasses must keep the parent's promises.
- **Interface segregation:** are interfaces small? A Payable interface with `charge()` beats a giant Terminal interface with printing, scanning and charging that every implementation must fake.
- **Dependency inversion:** do high-level classes depend on abstractions? Checkout receives a Pricing object in its constructor (**dependency injection**) instead of creating `Hourly` itself. Tests can pass a fake, and the business can swap rules without touching Checkout.

The code shows the before and after. The after version is not more clever; it is more boring, and that is the point. Each class is small, and the change the interviewer is most likely to ask for ("weekend rates", "members park free") is a new class plus one line where the object is built.

Do not apply every principle everywhere. An interface with exactly one implementation that will never vary is ceremony; a strategy for the thing the interviewer just told you will change is design. Say which parts you expect to vary and why, and spend your abstractions there. The activity asks you to add a pricing rule without touching Checkout at all.
sections.pitfall: Subclasses that break the parent's contract, such as overriding a method to raise NotImplementedError or to return a different type. Callers written for the parent then fail on the child, which is exactly what Liskov substitution forbids.

activity.title: Add a rule without editing Checkout
activity.prompt: Add a FirstHourFree class: the first hour is free, then every started hour costs rate. Do not change Checkout. Uncomment the two lines at the bottom and run it.

props.task: Write FirstHourFree, uncomment the last two lines, and make the output 9, 6 and 0.

check.question: Checkout creates `Hourly(3)` inside its own constructor. Which principle does injecting the Pricing object instead serve most directly?
choices: Interface segregation
Dependency inversion
Liskov substitution
Single responsibility
check.explanation: Dependency inversion says high-level code should depend on an abstraction that is handed in, not build a concrete class itself. Injection makes Checkout testable with a fake and lets callers choose the rule.

sections.title: Worked design: a parking lot
sections.body:
The activity holds a compact version of the whole parking lot, close to what you could write in about 15 minutes of an interview. Read it against the use cases from the requirements section, then run it.

- **Size** is an enum with ordered values, so "does this vehicle fit this spot?" is one comparison: `vehicle.size.value <= spot.size.value`.
- **Spot** knows its size and its current vehicle and answers `fits()`. The fit rule lives in exactly one place.
- **Ticket** links a vehicle, a spot and a start time.
- **ParkingLot** owns the spots, keeps active tickets in a dictionary keyed by plate (so `leave` is an O(1) lookup), and delegates the fee to the injected pricing object.

Two decisions worth saying out loud:

- **Smallest spot that fits.** The lot sorts its spots from small to large, so the first free spot that fits is the smallest one, which saves large spots for vans. Finding it is a linear scan, O(number of spots), fine for a few hundred spots. For a big garage, keep a pool of free spots per size (a set or deque for each Size) so parking and leaving are O(1) on average.
- **Time is a parameter.** `park` and `leave` take `now` instead of reading the clock, which makes the class easy to test ("leave at 2.5 hours") and is another small case of dependency injection.

What the interviewer will probably ask next, and how the design answers:

- "Add levels." A Level owns its spots, and ParkingLot owns levels and asks each one for a spot: composition again.
- "Add electric charging spots." ElectricSpot extends Spot and overrides `fits()` to also require an electric vehicle, returning False otherwise.
- "Two cars arrive at once." Finding a free spot and assigning it must happen as one step. In a multi-threaded program, guard that step with a lock (or let a database transaction do it) so two tickets can never share a spot.
- "Show free spots per size on the entrance sign." Add a counting method, or keep counters updated in `park` and `leave` if the sign reads them constantly. The activity asks for the counting method.
sections.tip: Keep "now" and other outside inputs as parameters in interview code. It makes your hand-tests short and your design easier to discuss.
sections.pitfall: Storing the same fact in two places, such as a spot's vehicle and a separate set of occupied spot IDs, without a single method that updates both. They drift apart, and the lot hands out an occupied spot.

activity.title: Run the parking lot
activity.prompt: Predict the printed spot IDs before you run it (the spots are passed in a scrambled order). Then add a free_count(size) method that returns how many empty spots of exactly that size there are, uncomment the last line, and run it again.

props.task: Add ParkingLot.free_count(size), uncomment the last line, and get 1 0 on the last line.

check.question: Why does ParkingLot keep active tickets in a dictionary keyed by license plate?
choices: So leave(plate) finds the ticket in O(1) instead of scanning every spot
Because dictionaries keep the spots sorted by size
So two cars with the same plate can park at once
Because Python lists cannot store objects
check.explanation: The leave use case starts from a plate, so a map from plate to ticket answers it in constant time on average, and the ticket points straight at the spot to free. Scanning every spot would be O(number of spots).

sections.title: Worked designs: a library and an elevator
sections.body:
**Library system.** After clarifying: members borrow and return copies, each member may hold at most three loans, loans last 14 days, and a member can place a hold on a title when no copy is free; the first member waiting gets the next returned copy.

The classes follow the nouns, as in the code block: Book (one per title), BookCopy (one per physical item, knows its current loan), Member (knows their loans), Loan (copy, member, due date, `is_overdue`) and Library (copies by ISBN, checkout, returns and holds). Holds are a **queue per ISBN**, a `deque`, because first come, first served is the fair rule and `popleft()` is O(1).

Two decisions to discuss. Limits such as `MAX_LOANS` and the loan period are policy: if students and faculty get different limits, move them into a LoanPolicy object that each kind of member supplies, rather than adding if-statements to checkout. And returning a copy must check the hold queue before putting the copy back on the shelf, which is exactly the bug in the activity.

**Elevator, at a high level.** This prompt is about states and decisions more than code volume.

- **Classes:** Elevator (current floor, direction, state, a set of stops), Request (a floor and direction from a hall button, or a destination floor from inside the car), a Dispatcher that assigns hall requests to cars, and a Building that owns the elevators.
- **State as an enum:** IDLE, MOVING_UP, MOVING_DOWN, DOORS_OPEN. Each `step()` moves one floor or opens the doors depending on the state and the stops. One state field keeps the rules in one place instead of scattered flags like `is_moving` and `going_up`.
- **Scheduling:** a simple, fair rule is to keep moving in the current direction while there are stops ahead, then reverse. It is the idea behind the SCAN disk scheduling algorithm, which is often called the elevator algorithm. Always serving the nearest request sounds faster but can leave someone at the far end waiting a long time.
- **Dispatching as a strategy:** pick the closest car already moving toward the floor in the right direction, or an idle one. Making the rule a strategy lets you swap in rush-hour or express-floor rules later.
- **Discuss rather than build:** buttons pressed while cars move (concurrency), weight limits and emergency stops. Interviewers want to hear you name them.
sections.tip: For any "design X" prompt, list the states something can be in. A state enum often reveals methods and rules you would otherwise miss.
sections.pitfall: Encoding a limit like MAX_LOANS as a magic number inside checkout. When the interviewer adds a second kind of member, the rule has nowhere to go but another if-statement.

activity.title: Serve the hold queue
activity.prompt: Ben places a hold while Ana has the only copy. Run it: after Ana returns the book, Ben still has nothing and the copy sits on the shelf. Fix return_copy so the first member in the hold queue gets the copy (keep the messages the same).

props.code:
from collections import deque

class Member:
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name, self.loans = name, []

class Library:
    def __init__(self, copies):
        self.free = dict(copies)            # isbn -> free copies
        self.holds = {}                     # isbn -> deque of members

    def checkout(self, isbn, member):
        if self.free.get(isbn, 0) == 0:
            self.holds.setdefault(isbn, deque()).append(member)
            return f"{member.name} is on hold for {isbn}"
        self.free[isbn] -= 1
        member.loans.append(isbn)
        return f"{member.name} borrowed {isbn}"

    def return_copy(self, isbn, member):
        member.loans.remove(isbn)
        self.free[isbn] += 1                # bug: ignores the holds
        return f"{member.name} returned {isbn}"

lib = Library({"dune": 1})
ana, ben = Member("Ana"), Member("Ben")
print(lib.checkout("dune", ana))
print(lib.checkout("dune", ben))
print(lib.return_copy("dune", ana))
print("Ben's loans:", ben.loans)
print("Free copies:", lib.free["dune"])
props.task: Change return_copy so the copy goes to the first member waiting, if any.
props.expectOutput:
Ana borrowed dune
Ben is on hold for dune
Ana returned dune
Ben's loans: ['dune']
Free copies: 0

check.question: Which data structure fits a hold list where the first member who asked gets the next returned copy?
choices: A stack
A set
A queue such as collections.deque
A sorted list by member name
check.explanation: First come, first served is FIFO, which is a queue; deque appends on the right and pops from the left in O(1). A stack would serve the newest hold first, and a set has no order at all.

sections.title: Designing an API: an LRU cache, and common mistakes
sections.body:
"Design an LRU cache" sits between a coding problem and an OOD problem: you design a small class API and implement it efficiently. A **least recently used** cache holds at most `capacity` items; when it is full, adding a new key evicts the key used longest ago. Reading a key counts as using it.

Start with the API, as you would in any OOD round:

- `LRUCache(capacity)`: reject a capacity of zero or less with an error.
- `get(key, default=None)`: return the value and mark the key as most recently used, or return the default when the key is missing.
- `put(key, value)`: insert or update, mark it as most recent, and evict the least recently used key if over capacity.

Both operations should be O(1). A dictionary alone finds keys in O(1) but does not track order; a list tracks order, but moving an item is O(n). The standard answer combines them: a **hash map from key to node** and a **doubly linked list** ordered from most to least recent. The map finds a node in O(1), and unlinking and relinking it is O(1) because each node knows both neighbors. **Sentinel** head and tail nodes remove the special cases for an empty list or the first and last item. Space is O(capacity). In Python, `collections.OrderedDict` packages the same idea with `move_to_end()` and `popitem(last=False)`; mention it, and be ready to build the linked list if asked.

Follow-ups to expect: thread safety (one lock around get and put, since both change the order), time-based expiry (store a timestamp per entry) and statistics such as hit rate (count in get).

**Common mistakes in OOD rounds:**

- Designing before asking a single question.
- A **god class** that does everything, such as a ParkingLot that also prints tickets, charges cards and sends emails.
- Inheritance for has-a relationships, or deep hierarchies for variations that a field or a strategy would cover.
- Strings instead of enums for fixed categories, so typos become bugs.
- Twenty classes and no working code: name the core, then write it.
- Patterns for their own sake: a factory, a builder and an observer where one constructor would do.
- Never saying trade-offs out loud: why a dictionary, why a queue, what changes at a larger scale.
sections.code:
class Node:
    def __init__(self, key=None, value=None):
        self.key, self.value = key, value
        self.prev = self.next = None

class LRUCache:
    """get and put in O(1): a dict finds nodes, a list keeps order."""

    def __init__(self, capacity):
        if capacity <= 0:
            raise ValueError("capacity must be positive")
        self.capacity = capacity
        self.nodes = {}                     # key -> Node
        self.head, self.tail = Node(), Node()   # sentinels
        self.head.next, self.tail.prev = self.tail, self.head

    def _unlink(self, node):
        node.prev.next, node.next.prev = node.next, node.prev

    def _push_front(self, node):            # most recently used
        node.prev, node.next = self.head, self.head.next
        self.head.next.prev = node
        self.head.next = node

    def get(self, key, default=None):
        node = self.nodes.get(key)
        if node is None:
            return default
        self._unlink(node)
        self._push_front(node)
        return node.value

    def put(self, key, value):
        if key in self.nodes:
            self._unlink(self.nodes[key])
        node = Node(key, value)
        self.nodes[key] = node
        self._push_front(node)
        if len(self.nodes) > self.capacity:
            lru = self.tail.prev            # least recently used
            self._unlink(lru)
            del self.nodes[lru.key]

cache = LRUCache(2)
cache.put("a", 1)
cache.put("b", 2)
cache.get("a")              # a is now the most recent
cache.put("c", 3)           # full: evicts b
print(cache.get("b"), cache.get("a"), cache.get("c"))  # None 1 3
cache.put("a", 10)          # update moves a to the front
cache.put("d", 4)           # evicts c
print(cache.get("c"), cache.get("a"), cache.get("d"))  # None 10 4
sections.tip: State the complexity of every public method when you finish an API: "get and put are O(1) on average, space is O(capacity)." It is the line interviewers wait for.
sections.pitfall: Forgetting that get counts as a use. If get does not move the key to the most recent position, the cache evicts keys that are being read constantly.

activity.title: Fix the eviction order
activity.prompt: This OrderedDict version evicts the wrong key: after a is read, adding c should evict b, not a. Run it, explain the output, then fix get so the last line prints None 1 3.

props.task: Make get mark the key as most recently used.

check.question: Which pair of structures gives an LRU cache O(1) get and put?
choices: A hash map from key to node plus a doubly linked list in recency order
A sorted array plus binary search
A min-heap keyed by insertion time
A singly linked list scanned from the head
check.explanation: The map finds a node in O(1), and the doubly linked list lets you unlink it and move it to the front in O(1). A heap needs O(log n) updates when an item is read, and scanning a list is O(n).

keyTerms.definition: An interview where you design the classes, responsibilities and methods for a system inside one program.
A short "actor does action" description of something the system must support.
A requirement about how well the system works, such as speed or safety under concurrency, rather than what it does.
A has-a relationship where the whole owns its parts and they share its lifetime.
A has-a relationship where the parts exist independently of the whole.
One object knowing or using another, without owning it.
How many objects take part in a relationship, written as 1, 0..1 or * for many.
Passing an object its collaborators, such as a pricing rule, instead of letting it create them.
A class that collects many unrelated responsibilities, so every change touches it.
A fixed-size cache that evicts the least recently used key when it is full.
A dummy node at the end of a linked list that removes special cases when linking and unlinking.

summary: An OOD round designs classes inside one program: clarify, list use cases, name classes and relationships, code the core, then handle changes.
Nouns in the use cases suggest classes and verbs suggest methods; put behavior with the data it needs.
Use composition for has-a, inheritance only for a true is-a, and enums for fixed categories.
A text class diagram with + and - members and <|--, *--, o-- and --> lines is enough to explain a design.
Apply SOLID where change is expected: inject a strategy for the rule the interviewer says will vary.
An LRU cache gets O(1) get and put from a hash map plus a doubly linked list; get must refresh recency.
lesson.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a friend how you would go from the prompt "design a library system" to a set of classes, including why Book and BookCopy are separate, where the loan limit rule should live and how holds are served.

questions.question: How does an object-oriented design round differ from a system design round?
choices: System design is only for frontend roles
OOD is about classes and methods inside one program; system design is about services, data stores and scale
They are the same round with different names
OOD never involves writing code
questions.explanation: OOD works inside one program: classes, responsibilities, relationships and methods. System design is about services, storage and scale across machines.

questions.question: Put the phases of a typical 45-minute OOD round in order.
items: Ask clarifying questions and list use cases
Name the core classes and relationships
Code the core classes and main methods
Handle the interviewer's changes and discuss trade-offs
questions.explanation: Requirements come first because the prompt is vague; classes and relationships come before code; the last minutes go to changes, edge cases and trade-offs.

questions.question: Which of these do interviewers usually look for in an OOD round? Choose all that apply.
choices: Clarifying requirements before designing
Classes with one clear responsibility each
Designs that absorb a likely change by adding code
Using as many design patterns as possible
A diagram of load balancers and database replicas
questions.explanation: Clarifying, clean abstractions, sensible relationships and extensibility are the core signals. Using as many patterns as possible and drawing infrastructure are common ways to lose points.

questions.question: The interviewer says, "Design a parking lot." What should you do first?
choices: Draw the database schema
Ask which design pattern they want
Start writing a Vehicle class
Ask a few clarifying questions and list the main use cases
questions.explanation: The prompt is deliberately vague, so the first few minutes go to questions and a use-case list. Starting with classes or code risks designing the wrong system.

questions.question: Which are useful clarifying questions for "design a parking lot"? Choose all that apply.
choices: Which vehicle types and spot sizes exist?
Can a car park in a larger spot when car spots are full?
How is the fee calculated, and might that change?
Is payment processing part of this design?
What color are the parking lines?
Which language does the card processor use internally?
questions.explanation: Questions about vehicle types, fit rules, fees and scope change the classes you need. The paint color and the programming language of the payment company do not.

questions.question: Which is a non-functional requirement for a parking lot system?
choices: Never assign the same spot to two cars arriving at the same moment
Show the number of free spots per size
Issue a ticket when a car parks
Compute the fee when a car leaves
questions.explanation: Non-functional requirements describe how well the system works, such as safety under concurrent arrivals. The others describe what it does, which makes them functional.

questions.question: What is a use case, and why write them down early in an OOD round?
questions.answer: A short "actor does action" sentence describing something the system must support, such as "a driver parks and gets a ticket". Written early, they fix the scope and become a checklist; their verbs become methods.
questions.explanation: Use cases turn a vague prompt into a checklist the interviewer has agreed to. Their nouns suggest classes and their verbs suggest methods, and walking them across the design later shows whether anything is missing.

questions.question: The interviewer says, "Your call," when you ask whether there are monthly passes. What is the best response?
choices: Silently include them and move on
Keep asking until they decide
Say "I'll leave monthly passes out for now and keep pricing pluggable so they can be added," then continue
Design every possible kind of pass
questions.explanation: Stating the assumption makes it a visible decision the interviewer can adjust. Silently assuming, or stalling, wastes the time the round gives you.

questions.question: Match each relationship to an example.

pairs.right: Loan and the Member who borrowed

questions.explanation: Inheritance is a genuine is-a, composition is owning a part that lives and dies with the whole, aggregation is having parts that exist on their own, and association is simply knowing or using another object.

questions.question: In a library design, should "due date" be its own class?
choices: Yes, with a DueDateManager to compute it
No, it is a field of Loan, and overdue logic lives on Loan
No, it should be a global variable
Yes, every noun becomes a class
questions.explanation: A due date has no behavior of its own here; it is data about a loan. Making it a class adds a box to explain without adding meaning. Loan.is_overdue uses it.

questions.question: Where should the method that answers "is this loan overdue?" live?
choices: On Member, because members borrow books
In a separate OverdueChecker class for every check
On Library, since it manages everything
On Loan, because Loan holds the due date
questions.explanation: Put behavior with the data it needs. Loan holds the due date, so Loan.is_overdue(today) is the natural home. Library or Member would have to reach into the loan to answer.

questions.question: Which pair is best modeled as aggregation rather than composition?
choices: A course and its enrolled students
A parking lot and its spots
A building and its floors
An order and its line items
questions.explanation: Course and Students: students exist independently and can join other courses. A building's floors, an order's line items and a lot's spots exist only as part of their whole, which is composition.

questions.question: Which Python standard-library module provides the class you subclass to define a fixed set of named values such as SMALL, COMPACT and LARGE?
questions.explanation: The enum module provides Enum. Members such as Size.LARGE cannot be misspelled the way strings can, and you can iterate over every option.

questions.question: Match each piece of text diagram notation to its meaning.

pairs.right: A has B but does not own it
A uses or refers to B

questions.explanation: The triangle in `<|--` points at the parent, the filled diamond in `*--` marks the owner in composition, the hollow diamond in `o--` marks aggregation, and `-->` is a plain association.

questions.question: What does `Spot --> "0..1" Vehicle` say about the design?
choices: Vehicle inherits from Spot
Every spot always has exactly one vehicle
A spot holds at most one vehicle, and may be empty
A vehicle can be in many spots
questions.explanation: "0..1" on the Vehicle side means each spot refers to zero or one vehicle: empty or occupied. A `"*"` would mean many.

questions.question: In a text class box, what do the leading `+` and `-` mean?
choices: + is a method, - is a field
+ is public, - is internal (private)
+ is static, - is instance
+ adds an item, - removes it
questions.explanation: Plus marks public members other classes may call, and minus marks internal ones. In Python the convention for internal names is a leading underscore.

questions.question: You finish your diagram. What is the best way to check it before coding?
choices: Add a class for every noun you skipped
Ask the interviewer to approve every line
Count the boxes; more is better
Walk each use case across it and see which object handles each step
questions.explanation: Walking each use case across the diagram shows which object receives each call and what it talks to. A use case with no clear home reveals a missing method or class.

questions.question: Match each SOLID principle to the design move that applies it.

pairs.right: Move fee calculation out of ParkingLot into Pricing
Add WeekendRate as a new Pricing class
ElectricSpot.fits returns False instead of raising
A small Payable interface with only charge()
Pass a Pricing object into Checkout's constructor

questions.explanation: Each principle answers a different question: one reason to change, adding without editing, safe substitution, small interfaces, and depending on abstractions that are passed in.

questions.question: Every new pricing rule means editing this function, and a typo in a vehicle type silently falls through. Which redesign fixes both problems?
choices: Use a Pricing interface with one class per rule, injected where needed, and an enum for vehicle types
Move the function into ParkingLot
Replace the strings with numbers 1, 2 and 3
Add an elif for every new vehicle type
questions.explanation: A Pricing interface with one class per rule makes new rules additions (open/closed), and an enum for vehicle types turns typos into immediate errors. More elif branches or a longer function keep both problems.

questions.question: ElectricSpot overrides fits() to raise an error when a gas car asks. Why is that a problem?
choices: ElectricSpot should not exist at all
It is fine, because errors are clearer than False
Callers that loop over spots expect True or False, so the subclass breaks the parent's contract and crashes them
Python does not allow overriding methods that return booleans
questions.explanation: Code written for Spot expects fits() to return True or False. A subclass that raises instead breaks that contract, so the park loop crashes the first time it meets an ElectricSpot. That is a Liskov substitution violation.

questions.question: Fill the blank so Checkout uses whatever pricing rule it is given.
choices: Pricing()
pricing
None
Hourly(3)
questions.explanation: Storing the injected object is dependency injection: Checkout depends on the Pricing interface, and the caller decides which rule to pass. Creating Hourly(3) inside would hard-code one rule.

questions.question: When is adding a Pricing interface with several implementations NOT worth it?
choices: When tests need a fake pricing rule
When members and non-members pay differently
When the interviewer said pricing will change
When there is exactly one rule that will never vary
questions.explanation: Abstractions pay off where change is expected. A rule that will never vary and has one implementation gains only ceremony from an interface. Say where you expect variation, and abstract there.

questions.question: Hourly pricing charges 3 per started hour, rounding up. What is the fee for 2.5 hours?
questions.explanation: Started hours round up: math.ceil(2.5) is 3, and 3 hours times 3 is 9.

questions.question: The lot sorts its spots from smallest to largest and takes the first free spot that fits. What does that achieve?
choices: Each vehicle gets the smallest spot that fits, saving large spots for vans
It guarantees the lot is never full
It sorts vehicles by plate number
It makes park O(1)
questions.explanation: With spots in ascending size, the first fit is the smallest fit, which keeps large spots free for vehicles that need them. It does not make the scan faster; it is still O(number of spots).

questions.question: A garage has 5,000 spots and park() scans them all. What change makes parking and leaving O(1) on average?
choices: Scan from the end of the list instead
Sort the spots by ID
Keep a free-spot pool per size and take from or return to it
Store spots in a longer list
questions.explanation: Keeping a pool of free spots per size (a set or deque for each Size) lets park take any free spot of the right size immediately, and leave puts the spot back. Sorting does not remove the scan, and a bigger list only makes it slower.

questions.question: Two threads call park() at the same moment and both pick spot 7. What is the fix?
choices: Use a list instead of a dict for tickets
Guard the find-and-assign step with a lock, so only one thread can claim a spot at a time
Ask drivers to arrive at different times
Check after parking and move one car
questions.explanation: Finding a free spot and marking it taken must be one atomic step. A lock around that step (or a database transaction) prevents two tickets for one spot. Retrying later or checking afterwards still leaves a window where both succeed.

questions.question: Why do park() and leave() take `now` as a parameter instead of reading the system clock?
choices: It makes the code run faster
Tickets cannot store timestamps otherwise
Reading the clock is not allowed in Python
It makes the class easy to test with exact times, a small form of dependency injection
questions.explanation: Passing time in makes tests simple and repeatable ("leave at 2.5 hours") without waiting or patching the clock. It is a small form of dependency injection.

questions.question: Students may borrow 3 books and faculty 10. Where should that rule live?
choices: A LoanPolicy object supplied by each kind of member and used by checkout
In the Book class
An if-statement in Library.checkout for each member type
A global constant MAX_LOANS = 10
questions.explanation: Limits are policy. A LoanPolicy that each kind of member supplies keeps checkout unchanged as rules grow (open/closed). Hard-coding if-statements in checkout means editing it for every new member type.

questions.question: A copy is returned while Ben is waiting on a hold, but Ben never gets it. What is wrong with return_copy?
choices: The free count should go down, not up
It should remove the loan from the book instead of the member
It never checks the hold queue; the first waiting member should get the copy
It should raise an error when someone is waiting
questions.explanation: The copy always goes back to the free count, so the hold queue is never served. return_copy should pop the first waiting member and give them the copy, and only increase the free count when nobody is waiting.

questions.question: Which is NOT a reasonable state for an elevator's state enum?
choices: DOORS_OPEN
THREE_PEOPLE_PRESSED_BUTTONS
IDLE
MOVING_UP
questions.explanation: IDLE, MOVING_UP and DOORS_OPEN describe what the car is doing. The number of people who pressed a button is data the dispatcher may track, not a state of the car.

questions.question: Why does the "keep going in the current direction, then reverse" elevator rule tend to be fairer than "always serve the nearest request"?
choices: It needs no state at all
Nearest-first is impossible to implement
It uses less electricity in every case
Nearest-first can starve a far-away request, while sweeping reaches every floor within about one round trip
questions.explanation: Nearest-first keeps serving whoever is close, so a request at the far end can wait a very long time. Sweeping in one direction guarantees every floor is reached within about one round trip.

questions.question: Put the steps of handling a hall call in a simple elevator design in order.
items: A rider presses the up button on floor 5
A Request for floor 5, direction up, is created
The Dispatcher assigns it to the best car
That car adds floor 5 to its stops
The car moves floor by floor and opens its doors at 5
questions.explanation: A button press creates a Request, the Dispatcher picks a car, that car adds a stop, and its step loop moves floor by floor until it opens the doors at the stop.

questions.question: An LRU cache has capacity 2. You put a, put b, get a, then put c. Which key is evicted?
questions.explanation: Reading a makes it the most recent, so b is now the least recently used and is evicted when c arrives.

questions.question: Why does the linked-list LRU cache use sentinel head and tail nodes?
choices: Every real node always has neighbors, so linking and unlinking need no special cases
They make the cache thread-safe
Python requires them for doubly linked lists
They store the most and least used values
questions.explanation: Dummy nodes at both ends mean every real node always has a previous and a next node, so insert and unlink never need special cases for an empty list or the first and last item.

questions.question: Which are common mistakes in object-oriented design interviews? Choose all that apply.
choices: Designing before asking any questions
One class that parks cars, prints tickets, charges cards and sends emails
Inheriting ParkingLot from Level to reuse its spots
Using strings like "lrg" for spot sizes
Explaining why you chose a dictionary over a list
questions.explanation: Skipping requirements, god classes, inheritance for has-a and strings for fixed categories all cost points. Stating trade-offs is what interviewers want to hear.

questions.question: What is a god class, and what is the usual fix?
choices: A class with a long name; rename it
A class with only static methods; make them instance methods
A class that does many unrelated jobs; split it into focused classes with one responsibility each
A base class with many subclasses; delete the subclasses
questions.explanation: A god class gathers many unrelated responsibilities, so every change touches it. Splitting it into focused classes, each with one reason to change, is the single responsibility principle at work.

questions.question: An interviewer asks how to make your LRU cache safe when several threads call get and put. What is the best answer?
choices: Lock only put, because get only reads
Hold one lock for the whole of each get and put, because both change the recency order
Nothing; dictionaries are always thread-safe
Give each thread its own cache and never share it
questions.explanation: Both get and put modify the recency order, so both must be protected. One lock around each whole operation is the simple, correct answer; reads that move nodes are not read-only.

questions.question: In an OOD round you have named 14 classes after 25 minutes and written no code. What should you do?
choices: Start over with a different design
Ask the interviewer which classes to delete
Keep adding classes until the design is complete
Pick the core classes behind the main use cases and code their key methods now
questions.explanation: A design with no code behind it is hard to evaluate. Pick the few classes that carry the main use cases, write their key methods, and mention the rest as extensions.
